Proof. Suppose α algebraic. For each such N, the dyadic truncation
p_N / 2^N := Σ_{a_n ≤ N} 2^{−a_n} is a rational with S-unit denominator
(S = {2}). The tail satisfies
  0 < α − p_N/2^N = Σ_{a_n > N} 2^{−a_n} ≤ Σ_{k>N+L(N)} 2^{−k}
                  = 2^{−(N+L(N))} · 2 = 2^{−(N+L(N))+1},
using exactly that no 1-position lies in (N, N+L(N)]. Since L(N) ≥ εN,
  |α − p_N/2^N| ≤ 2^{−(1+ε)N + 1} = 4 · 2^{−(1+ε)N}.
Ridout's theorem (Ridout 1957, p-adic extension of Roth; S = {2}, the
denominator 2^N is an S-unit) states: for algebraic irrational α and
every δ > 0 there are only finitely many rationals p/q with q an
S-unit and |α − p/q| < q^{−2−δ}. Take δ = ε/2: the displayed bound is
< 2^{−(2+ε/2)N} for all large N in the infinite family, and each 2^N
is an S-unit denominator — infinitely many such approximations, i.e.
|α − p_N/2^N| < (2^N)^{−2−ε/2} infinitely often. Contradiction. Hence
α is transcendental. Hypotheses verified: α irrational is forced (a
rational has eventually periodic binary expansion, contradicting
limsup aₙ/n = ∞ ⇒ unbounded gaps ⇒ aperiodicity); Ridout's exact
published hypotheses (algebraic irrational α, S finite set of primes,
S-unit denominators, exponent 2+δ) are each matched. ∎
